{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"325-9B(1) lists which uses need a special permit (cemeteries, schools, hospitals, home occupations, towers and so on) and sets criteria for exempting home occupations and antennas. It does not limit a design through the available measures. Whether a use needs a special permit is a procedural trigger, not a dimension, and the home-occupation criteria (stock of merchandise, traffic, exterior display, noise) and the antenna conditions (diameter, 10 ft height, front yard, screening) cannot be decided from the listed measures. Subsection (2) sends signage to Chapter 272 and (3) sends additional conditions to §325-10, and both are drafted from those sections. Making rules from this text would need new measures and judgment calls on undefined words such as 'incidental', 'objectionable effects' and 'visible'. Those are not set out in 325-9B itself, so I did not draft any template."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"This piece is a definition. Its sentence 'Any dwelling unit occupied by a cooperative household shall be considered a multiple dwelling' classifies the use. It sets no limit, minimum, prohibition or condition on a design that code can check with the listed measures. We have no measure for whether a household is a cooperative household, and the classification feeds into the use-type rules (multiple_family chart rows) rather than being a requirement itself. The last sentence, which excludes supervised residential care facilities such as halfway houses, hostels or group homes, limits the definition's scope. It is not a design requirement, and it would need an architect's judgment about the use. The occupancy rules (four or more unrelated persons) are drafted from the occupancy sections of the law, not from here."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"This is a definition of \"functional family unit\". Its requirements are about who occupies a dwelling unit (the shared unit, household stability, college students, unrelated adults, minor dependent children), and none of the listed measures can decide them. The listed measures cover lot size, yards, height, parking and unit counts, not occupants. The stability criteria in (1)(b) need judgment. The presumptions in (2) and (3) can be rebutted by evidence under (4). The text sets no dimensional or design requirement on a building. Occupancy limits are drafted where the chart or the law sets them (chart footnote 1 on page 2 and the occupancy restrictions in §325-3), not from this definition."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"The OCCUPANT definition is for R-2c only, and its requirements can't be decided from the listed measures. There is no measure for occupants, habitable square footage, sleeping-room area or kitchen area, and the text doesn't say what 'appropriate lot size requirements' are. A formula would need guesses, which risks a false pass. Subsection (1) is a definition and subsection (4) is an exclusion from it; neither sets a limit on a design. Subsection (2)'s table and subsection (3)'s limit on sleeping more persons need new measures and answers from the architects. These questions are open: how habitable space is measured, and which lot size requirements (the chart's per-occupant minimum lot size in footnotes 4-6) apply. The R-2c chart footnotes 4-6 on page 3 set the lot-size-by-occupant rules and belong to the chart rows, not to this piece."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"This text is a definition of a TRAILER OR TRAVEL TRAILER, not a requirement on a building design. The phrase 'limited in width to eight feet in length to 32 feet' describes the kind of portable unit the term covers (together with being towable and designed as a temporary dwelling). It does not limit anything an architect designs on a lot. The measures available (use, lot, yards, building height and so on) cannot describe a trailer's width or length, and none of the listed use ids is a trailer. The wording is also garbled ('eight feet in length to 32 feet'), so any formula would need an interpretation, which belongs in an open question and not in a check. The residential districts get no rule from this piece. It needs to be handled as a definition, and any use or parking restriction on trailers should be drafted from the section of the law that sets it."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Piece 325-8D sets requirements only for the CBD districts: the CBD-50 historic review, the stepback in the CBD-85 District on the 100 block of West Green Street, and the active-use requirement on storefronts fronting the Primary Commons or the mapped street-level active use zone. None of these apply to the residential districts listed (R-1a, R-1b, R-2a, R-2b, R-2c, R-3a, R-3aa, R-3b, RU). The CBD district is not one of the residential districts, and the active-use condition also depends on a map and on use categories we don't have as measures. So no rule can be drafted for the residential districts."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Piece 325-10C sets conditions on special permits that the available measures cannot decide. Most are operational or judgment-based: hours of operation, machinery size, refuse handling, nuisance, compatibility, owner-management, board discretion, and annual review. The neighborhood garden provisions that look measurable (the 64 sf structure caps, the 8 ft right-of-way, one parking space per 15 plots) depend on facts that are not in the measure list: garden plot counts, shelter floor area and right-of-way width. The use list has no neighborhood garden use id, and the bed-and-breakfast conditions need facts such as owner-management and exterior alterations that no measure covers. I have not drafted rules that would need new measures and a use id that cannot be verified, to avoid a false pass."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Every requirement in 325-27D depends on facts that are not among the available measures: whether the use is a short-term rental, whether the host's primary residence is on the property, whether the unit is owner-occupied, the dwelling or building type, whether the host is a natural person, whether a permit is held, and whether there is written owner authorization. With none of these measurable, code could not decide any of them. The text sets no chart numbers, and the only measures that come close are dwelling_units and the use ids. The use measure has no short-term rental value and cannot tell a single-family unit from a unit inside a multiple dwelling or mixed-use building. Drafting a rule on those measures would settle the unclear points in the formula, which risks a false pass. The text also sets no dimensional limit on a design. Subsection (1), permission only in zones where residential uses are allowed, depends on the use tables of other sections. The permit (4), natural-person (5) and authorization (2)(b) requirements are procedures and applicant eligibility, not requirements on a building design. Subsection (6), no limit on rental days, is a permission and sets no requirement. Subsection (3) restricts the dwelling types in which short-term rentals are allowed, and would need new measures for short-term rental use, owner-occupancy and the building type. It also depends on §325-28 and the ADU definition for what counts as an ADU."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Every requirement in 325-27F is about the operation or administration of a short-term rental: permit and certificate upkeep, tax remittance, posting notices, listing the permit number, and naming a local contact. Maximum occupancy is also stated, but it is set by the certificate of compliance rather than by a number in the text, and no listed measure holds the certificate's occupancy or the number of occupants. Each of these items depends on facts such as permit status, certificate occupancy, postings, listings and contact presence, and none of these is among the available design measures. They cannot be tested against a building design with the measures available, and no check could avoid guessing. Without a measure or a worked example to tie them to, a rule or flag here would add nothing and could produce a false pass."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"The measures available cannot decide any requirement in 325-29.1D, so no template can be drafted from them. The piece covers adult uses, and none of the listed use ids is an adult use. The requirements are: location only within the Adult Use Overlay Zone, and distances of 350 feet or 200 feet from residential district boundaries, day-care facilities, religious or educational structures, waterfronts, parks, farmers' markets, gymnastic centers, libraries, museums and Marine Commercial Districts. They need measures for the overlay zone and for distances to those features, and the measure list has none. A rule would need a measure that does not exist, and a rule on a non-existent adult use cannot be checked. Also, the piece is not a limit on the design of residential lots. It concerns where adult uses may open and is tied to the Adult Use Overlay Zone, and the listed residential districts do not allow adult uses. The distances are measured from the boundary of residential zoning districts, so they restrict adult-use siting, not residential development."}

Whether a site is an opportunity site or avoidance area depends on city maps, aerial photographs and officials' determinations (L64-L66), and the Landmarks Commission must approve any PWSF in an avoidance area under A(3)(b) (L70-L72). The 15 ft equipment height and 20 ft alley setback apply only in special interest areas, which have no measure here. A rule would need new measures and a facility type that the engineers have not defined, so no template is drafted."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"325-29.12B tells the Board of Zoning Appeals what its written decisions on wireless facility (PWSF) applications must specify: whether there is a significant coverage gap, whether the installation is the least intrusive means, aesthetic impact, fall zone, alternatives, and consistency with legislative intent. These are findings the Board makes on evidence, and they are decision procedure, not dimensional requirements on a building design. None of the available measures (lot area, yards, height, use ids, parking and the like) covers a wireless facility, and no use id covers wireless facilities. The measurable elements named in the text (drive test data, minimum necessary height, fall zone) set no number and need judgment about evidence, so code can't decide them. Any flag would have no check and would apply to no residential-district design measure. The text sets no requirement that code can check for the residential districts listed, so I return no templates."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Piece 325-32A sets no limit that code can check against the measurements we have. It lets a lawfully established nonconforming use, building or lot continue \"so long as the nonconformity remains otherwise lawful and complies with this section\". Whether a nonconformity is \"otherwise lawful\" is a legal judgment with no listed measure. \"This section\" refers to the rest of §325-32 and to related sections (325-35A permits, 325-20C parking, 325-32C), which are drafted from their own text. Folding them in here would settle in a formula what belongs to those sections. A rule with check \"\" would be a flag, but a flag with no check adds nothing the other sections' rules don't already give. The second sentence, that rights run with the property and are not affected by changes in tenancy or ownership, is a statement of legal effect. It sets no requirement on a building design. Open questions for the architects: what \"otherwise lawful\" covers, and which later provisions of §325-32 \"complies with this section\" brings in."}

It sets design review and approval sequencing (Planning and Development Board review under Chapter 160, Landmarks Preservation Commission recommendation before final action on demolition, and prior approval as a prerequisite for the Director and Board of Zoning Appeals). Those are procedures and judgments, not measurable requirements on a design in a residential district, so no rule or flag applies to the residential districts."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Piece 325-45.1C applies only to the Collegetown Area Form Districts, which are not among the residential districts listed (R-1a, R-1b, R-2a, R-2b, R-2c, R-3a, R-3aa, R-3b, RU). {"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"325-12D sets no requirement that code can decide from the listed measures for the residential districts. Subsection (1) permits PUD land to be used for any lawful purpose permitted in the zone where it is located, plus any other uses the Common Council may authorize. Whether a use is permitted in the underlying zone depends on the use chart, which is drafted elsewhere. The measures also do not say whether a lot is in a PUD or whether the Council has authorized a use. Subsection (2) defers yard size, height, building coverage and lot size to the rezoning legislation for each PUD and lets the Common Council impose conditions. That legislation is not in the documents given, so no number can be drawn from it. Both subsections are discretionary or defer to other documents, and any rule would need a guess, which risks a false pass. The PUD requirements should be handled through the PUD rezoning legislation, or as a flag raised when a design is in a PUD."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"325-12H lets the Common Council impose conditions on a PUD rezoning in its legislative discretion, such as limiting uses, locations and sizes of buildings, providing open space and recreation areas, and requiring bonds or assurances for infrastructure. It sets no limit, minimum, prohibition or condition that a design can be measured against. Any condition arises only when the Council imposes it in a particular rezoning, so there is nothing for code to check. The text is also a procedure-like grant of discretion, and it applies to PUD rezonings, not to the listed residential districts' chart requirements. Any flag would be a placeholder with no measurable content, so no templates are drafted."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Piece 325-15A sets only requirements that the available measures cannot decide. The measures cover lot size, yards, height, coverage and parking. None of them records whether topsoil is removed, whether grading or tree removal has started, whether a building permit has been issued, or whether a watercourse is altered. The topsoil rule turns on judgment (erosion or flooding risk, whether the remaining topsoil is adequate for typical vegetation), and the remainder needs approval from the Director of Planning and Development or the City Engineer. These are permit and procedure prerequisites, not dimensions of a building design, so they can't be turned into a pass/fail check without inventing measures. I did not draft a flag template because a flag needs a quote and an applies_when, and none of this belongs to the residential chart rows; the topsoil, grading and watercourse requirements are better handled as construction-phase permit conditions."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Every requirement in 325-24B needs a fact that is not among the measures we have: whether the use produces or processes materials, what is stored, whether a barrier or screen exists, and how waste is stored. The standards in L1-L5, 'not injurious or offensive', and in L8-L13, 'effectively screened', depend on human judgment. The measures listed (lot dimensions, yards, height, parking and so on) can't decide any of them. The text sets no number. The rule lives in the use and operation of a site, not in the building's dimensions. A rule here would need new measures such as waste_storage_enclosed, and it would not apply to every lot, only to uses where 325-24B is referenced. The residential-district chart does not say that any residential district refers to this section. These requirements are better left for an architect's review than drafted as rules that could give a false pass."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"325-24C sets no requirement that code can decide from the available measures. Its first sentence limits sound levels at the lot line to \"standards prescribed by the American Standards Association\". It gives no numeric limit and the ASA standard is not in the law text, and no sound-level measure exists, so the design cannot be checked against it. The second sentence (objectionable noises from intermittence, beat frequency or shrillness shall be muffled so as not to become a nuisance to adjacent uses) needs an architect's judgment and cannot be measured. Open questions for the architects: which ASA standard and edition applies, and what the limit is. How does 325-24C relate to the overlapping noise provision in 325-23A(1)? What counts as \"muffled\" and \"nuisance to adjacent uses\"? Neither point can be settled in a formula."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"325-24D prohibits ground vibration that is \"perceptible without instruments\" at any point along the lot lines. The reviewed label already marks the text as a flag for an architect's judgment, so I drafted no template."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Piece 325-29.11A sets no measurable requirement on a building design in the residential districts. It describes what alternatives to a proposed PWSF (personal wireless service facility) in an application review should contain. The alternatives \"need not be totally different\" and \"should contain measurable differences, such as\" height, number, location, siting and design. Each of these is a permissive example (\"can be\", \"could be\"), and \"should\" is guidance for what an applicant submits. It does not limit a lot, a yard, a height or a use, and none of the listed measures (lot, yards, height, stories, parking, units) can test it. The text also has no number of its own to type. It is procedural content for the application review, so it gives no rule template, and no flag is needed for the districts listed."}

{"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"Piece 325-29.11C sets no requirement a design can be checked against. This is a procedure for staff, and each criterion calls for human judgment. None sets a limit, minimum, prohibition or condition, and none can be measured with the available measures. The text also names no residential district and sets no number. The listed measures (lot dimensions, yards, height, stories, parking and so on) do not cover any of the criteria. {"templates":[],"no_rule_reason":"325-29.21B sets nothing that code can decide with the listed measures, and it names no residential district. Each sentence fails for a specific reason. (1) 'A security barrier ... may be required around the perimeter of mount(s) or equipment structure, and any anchor points' is permissive (may be required), so it sets no fixed requirement. It also refers to the 'City of Ithaca Zoning Ordinance' for the barrier standard, and that standard is not in the text given. (2) 'In the case of a roof-mounted PWSF, the security barrier may need only be around the antenna' is a permitted reduction, not a measurable limit. (3) 'The security barrier shall be maintained by the operator of the PWSF or mount for the life of the installation' is an ongoing maintenance duty owed by the operator. It cannot be tested against a building design's measurements. (4) 'No security barrier is needed around side-mounted PWSF's' is an exemption.
